steps.tx: **Sleep architecture** describes the structural cyclical organization of nocturnal sleep, cycling continuously between non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) phases. A healthy human adult experiences four to six complete 90- to 120-minute cycles per night, with deep slow-wave sleep predominating early and REM episodes expanding toward morning.
steps.say: Sleep architecture cycles through NREM and REM stages every ninety to one hundred and twenty minutes, with deep sleep dominating early and REM expanding near dawn.

left.title: NREM Sleep (Stages N1-N3)
points: Seventy-five to eighty percent of total sleep

right.title: REM Sleep (Dreaming)
points: Twenty to twenty-five percent of total sleep
Vivid visual dreams and penile tumescence

steps.tx: An overnight hypnogram plots stage against clock time and shows four to six full cycles. Each cycle lasts about ninety to one hundred twenty minutes, alternating non-rapid eye movement sleep with rapid eye movement sleep. Deep slow-wave sleep fills the early cycles, while rapid eye movement stretches longer toward morning. That repeating pattern is normal **sleep architecture** in a healthy adult.
steps.say: An overnight hypnogram plots stage against clock time and shows four to six full cycles. Each cycle lasts about ninety to one hundred twenty minutes, alternating non-rapid eye movement sleep with rapid eye movement sleep. Deep slow-wave sleep fills the early cycles, while rapid eye movement stretches longer toward morning. That repeating pattern is normal sleep architecture in a healthy adult.

vis.alt: Overnight hypnogram with four to six NREM and REM cycles, slow-wave early and longer REM later
vis.caption: An overnight hypnogram traces repeated NREM and REM cycles, with deep slow-wave sleep early and longer REM episodes later. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **NREM sleep stages** subdivide into N1, N2, and N3 based on electroencephalographic frequency and wave morphology. Stage N1 is a light transitional phase with theta waves; Stage N2 displays distinctive 12 to 14 Hertz sleep spindles and high-voltage K-complexes; Stage N3 features low-frequency delta waves under 4 Hertz.
steps.say: NREM progresses from light N1 theta waves to N2 with sleep spindles and K-complexes, culminating in N3 delta slow-wave restorative sleep.

vis.title: NREM Stage Characteristics
rows: Fifty percent of total sleep; memory consolidation
Growth hormone secretion; highest arousal threshold

steps.tx: **REM sleep physiology** features intense cerebral metabolic activity, bursts of rapid conjugate eye movements, and profound somatic muscle atonia mediated by descending glycine and GABAergic inhibition from the locus subcoeruleus onto spinal alpha motor neurons. Nocturnal penile tumescence occurs regularly, distinguishing psychogenic from organic erectile dysfunction.
steps.say: REM sleep features rapid eye movements, vivid dreams, penile tumescence, and profound somatic muscle atonia mediated by spinal glycinergic inhibition.

left.title: Active Cerebral Features
points: Bursts of rapid conjugate eye movements

steps.tx: **Polysomnography monitoring**, abbreviated PSG, is the gold standard diagnostic recording modality in sleep medicine, conducted in an overnight sleep laboratory. Standard comprehensive montages combine electroencephalography for sleep staging, electrooculography for eye movements, electromyography for muscle tone, electrocardiography for heart rate, and nasal airflow pressure sensors.
steps.say: Overnight polysomnography combines EEG, eye tracking, chin EMG, ECG, and respiratory sensors to objectively diagnose sleep disorders.

vis.title: Polysomnography Sensor Montage
rows: Defines N1, N2, N3, and REM stage transitions
Detects slow roving movements (N1) vs rapid bursts (REM)
Submental chin and bilateral anterior tibialis
Confirms REM atonia; detects restless legs twitches
Quantifies apnoeas and hypopnoeas per sleep hour

steps.tx: Zoom into the EEG epoch itself and stage N2 announces itself with two brief graphoelements against a low voltage background. Short waxing and waning bursts are sleep spindles, while a sharp negative wave followed by a slower positive component forms a **K-complex**. Recognising both lets the scorer separate true N2 from drowsy N1 and from the high amplitude slow waves dominating deeper N3 sleep stages.
steps.say: Stage N2 is recognised by sleep spindles and K-complexes on the EEG. These graphoelements separate N2 from drowsy N1 and deeper slow wave sleep.

vis.alt: Polysomnography EEG epoch displaying sleep spindles and a K-complex characteristic of stage N2 sleep
vis.caption: An EEG epoch from polysomnography shows sleep spindles and a K-complex marking stage N2 sleep. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Insomnia disorder** is characterized by persistent difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep with frequent nocturnal awakenings, or early morning awakening with inability to return to sleep. The disturbance occurs despite adequate sleep opportunity at least three nights per week for at least three months, causing daytime fatigue.
steps.say: Insomnia requires sleep difficulty occurring at least three nights weekly for three months despite adequate opportunity, causing impaired daytime functioning.

vis.title: Insomnia Phenotypes
rows: High autonomic arousal and generalized anxiety
Sleep apnoea, chronic pain, or alcohol misuse
Waking >=2 hours before desired alarm time
Classic biological hallmark of melancholic depression

steps.tx: **Narcolepsy tetrad** is a chronic neurological sleep disturbance caused by the selective autoimmune destruction of approximately 70,000 hypocretin (orexin) producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. The classic clinical tetrad comprises excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, and transient sleep paralysis upon awakening.
steps.say: Narcolepsy stems from lateral hypothalamic orexin loss, producing daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, vivid sleep-wake hallucinations, and sleep paralysis.

nodes.label: Autoimmune destruction of lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons
Loss of wakefulness stabilization across ascending arousal networks
Abrupt daytime intrusions of REM phenomena into alert consciousness
Irresistible sleep attacks, sudden cataplexy, & hypnagogic visions

steps.tx: **Cataplexy** is the pathognomonic clinical feature of narcolepsy type 1, defined as sudden, transient, bilateral loss of skeletal muscle tone provoked by strong emotions, most commonly hearty laughter, joking, or surprise. Consciousness remains fully alert and preserved throughout the brief collapse, distinguishing cataplexy from epileptic atonic seizures.
steps.say: Cataplexy is sudden bilateral muscle collapse provoked by laughter while consciousness remains fully alert, distinguishing it from epilepsy.

left.title: Cataplexy (Narcolepsy Type 1)
points: Provoked by hearty laughter or surprise
Bilateral knee buckling or jaw drooping

right.title: Atonic Epileptic Seizure
points: Ictal EEG shows generalized polyspike discharges

steps.tx: **Multiple Sleep Latency Test**, abbreviated MSLT, confirms narcolepsy by demonstrating pathological daytime sleepiness across five scheduled 20-minute nap opportunities conducted at two-hour intervals. Diagnostic criteria require a mean sleep onset latency under eight minutes and the presence of two or more sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs).
steps.say: The MSLT confirms narcolepsy by demonstrating sleep onset in under eight minutes and at least two sleep-onset REM episodes across five naps.

vis.title: MSLT Diagnostic Criteria
rows: >= 2 SOREMPs (or 1 on MSLT plus 1 on prior PSG)
